questions.question: A function loops over array `a` (length a) and, inside that loop, over array `b` (length b). What is its time complexity?
questions.explanation: Nested loops multiply. Because the arrays have different sizes, use separate letters: O(a × b). Sequential loops would add to O(a + b).

questions.question: Why is `array.push` described as amortised O(1)?
options: Occasional resizes copy the array, but capacity grows geometrically so the total copying over n pushes is O(n)
questions.explanation: A resize is O(n), but it happens rarely because capacity doubles (or grows by a factor). Spread over all pushes, the average cost per push is constant.

questions.question: The input limit says n can be up to 10⁵. Which approach is most likely too slow?
options: O(n log n) sorting followed by one pass
O(n) single pass with a hash map
O(log n) binary search per query for a few queries
questions.explanation: 10⁵ squared is 10¹⁰ operations, far beyond what runs in a second or two. O(n) and O(n log n) fit comfortably.

questions.question: What is the space complexity of `function sumTo(n) { return n === 0 ? 0 : n + sumTo(n - 1); }`?
options: O(n), because n calls are pending on the call stack at the deepest point
O(1), because it creates no arrays
questions.explanation: Each recursive call waits for the next one, so up to n stack frames exist at once. That is O(n) extra space even though no array is created.
